claims.text: Spark plasma sintering can be used for in-situ reactive sintering of blended refractory high-entropy alloy and copper powders.
SPS processing will produce a refined microstructure in the RHEA–copper composite.
SPS processing will produce a stable microstructure in the RHEA–copper composite.
SPS rapidly initiates reactions at the interfaces between the refractory alloy and copper.
Rapidly initiated interfacial reactions mitigate phase segregation associated with a high positive heat of mixing.
The initial material is a homogeneously mixed blend of RHEA constituents and copper powder.
Rapid heating and short sintering durations can promote reaction while limiting grain growth.
Rapid heating and short sintering durations can limit phase segregation.
SPS will form well-bonded interfacial regions between the refractory ensemble and copper.
SPS may produce fine, evenly distributed intermetallic phases in the composite.
Rapid heating accelerates in-situ chemical reactions at RHEA–copper interfaces.
The shortened high-temperature exposure limits the time available for detrimental phase segregation.
The shortened high-temperature exposure limits excessive grain growth.
High positive heats of mixing typically induce detrimental phase segregation and excessive grain growth in this processing context.
The SPS composite will have a finer microstructure than a conventionally sintered composite.
The SPS composite will have a more homogeneous microstructure than a conventionally sintered composite.
The SPS composite will have improved interfacial bonding relative to a conventionally sintered composite.
Traditional sintering generally produces larger grains and more phase segregation because of prolonged high-temperature exposure.
The proposed advantages may diminish when temperature or time deviates substantially from optimized conditions.
The proposed advantages may diminish when the powder particle-size distribution is nonuniform.
